title: Splitting and quoting command lines
description:
Write both halves of lesson 5.03's quoting rules, so that a program you start receives exactly the arguments you meant:

```cpp
std::vector<std::string> splitCommandLine(const std::string& line);
std::string quoteArgument(const std::string& arg);
std::string buildCommandLine(const std::vector<std::string>& args);
```

**splitCommandLine** follows the C runtime's rules:
- Spaces and tabs outside quotes separate arguments (several in a row count as one); they are not part of any argument.
- A `"` switches quoting on or off and is not part of the argument. An argument can be partly quoted: `a" b"c` is one argument, `a bc`. `""` alone is an empty argument.
- Backslashes are literal, except **directly before** a `"`: then `2n` backslashes become `n` backslashes and the `"` switches quoting; `2n + 1` backslashes become `n` backslashes and a literal `"`.

**quoteArgument** returns the argument unchanged if it is not empty and contains no space, tab or `"`. Otherwise it wraps it in quotes, writing each `"` as `\"` with the backslashes before it doubled, and doubling the backslashes at the very end (before the closing quote).

**buildCommandLine** quotes each argument and joins them with single spaces. For every list of arguments, `splitCommandLine(buildCommandLine(args)) == args`.
hints: In the splitter, read a whole run of backslashes at once and look at the character after it; that is the only place the rules need to know how many there were.
In the quoter, count backslashes as you go and decide how many to write only when you see what comes after them: a quote, an ordinary character, or the end.
